(i) The signal‐intensity distribution in a 300 MHz head‐sized sample depends on the excitation and reception coil distributions, and (ii) The signal‐receiving efficiency is proportional to the amplitude of the B _{1} field rotating in the opposite sense to that of precession, which is the circularly polarised component rotating in the same direction as precession.

the signal intensity distribution in an excitation‐only experiment is the same as the B1 field magnitude distribution and that the signal intensity is proportional to the B1 field circularly polarized in a direction opposite to that in which the spins precess.
the excitation and reception fields of a 10‐ cm diameter surface coil are different, and that this difference results in different excitation, reception, and signal intensity distributions.

the study of the RF field distribution in the head at high field.
understanding and controlling the B1 field distribution in a head‐sizing phantom excited at 300 MHz by a single loop surface coil.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in a single‐loop surface coil system the excitation and reception fields are not the same and that the reception field is proportional to the circularly polarizated component of the B _{1} field that rotates in a direction opposite to that for the nuclear precession.

the signal intensity in a spherical phantom excited with a circularly polarized RF magnetic field at 300 MHz is determined by the magnitude of the component of the RF field that rotates in a direction opposite to that which the nuclear magnetization precesses.

the signal intensity distribution in this system is determined by the product of the excitation and reception field distributions and is proportional to the square of the circularly polarization of the B1 component that rotates in the opposite direction of nuclear precession.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the case of a single‐loop coil at 300 MHz, the signal intensity distribution is not simply proportional to the B1 field magnitude distribution.
the excitation and reception of the RF fields are not always the same.
the B _{1} field is complex, that it is not a simple dipole, and that it is important to separate excitation and receptivity in order to understand signal intensity distributions.

it is important to think about the separate excitation distribution and reception distribution when considering the signal intensity distribution at high frequencies.
